scenarios.name: single filer, CSRS pension, age 60 (below the general 65 threshold, not disabled): correctly no deduction either way -- contrast/regression case
scenarios.source: Idaho Form 39R Instructions 2025 (EFO00088), page 7, 'Line 8 Retirement Benefits Deduction', 'Part One - Age, Disability, and Marital/Filing Status': 'The recipients must be at least age 65 or be classified as disabled and be at least age 62.' At age 60 and not disabled, this taxpayer fails Part One entirely, so no deduction is available regardless of the pension's source. Arithmetic: federal standard deduction (age 60, not 65+, no OBBBA senior bonus) = $16,100 base only. $40,000 - $16,100 = $23,900 taxable x 5.3% flat rate = $1,266.70.

scenarios.name: single filer, CSRS pension, age 68 (above the general 65 threshold): qualifies for the Retirement Benefits Deduction, engine grants nothing
scenarios.source: Idaho Form 39R Instructions 2025 (EFO00088), page 7-8: Part One (age 65+ satisfied at 68), Part Two 'Qualified Retirement Benefits': 'Civil Service Employees: Retirement annuities paid by the U.S. Civil Service Retirement System (CSRS)...To qualify for the deduction, the employee must have established eligibility before 1984.' Page 7, Line 8a: maximum deductible for 2025 is $48,216 single, reduced dollar-for-dollar by Social Security/Railroad Retirement Act benefits received (none in this fixture). This fixture stipulates the CSRS eligibility (established before 1984) in prose, as ClassifiedPensionSource has no field for it. Arithmetic: standard deduction (age 68, 65+) = $16,100 base + $2,050 age-65 addition + $6,000 full OBBBA senior bonus (MAGI $40,000 under the $75,000 threshold) = $24,150. $40,000 - $24,150 = $15,850 before the retirement deduction. The $40,000 CSRS pension is eligible up to the lesser of itself or $48,216, i.e. the full $40,000, which exceeds the $15,850 remaining and floors taxable income at $0. Tax = $0.00.

knownDefect.summary: CSRS retirement annuities qualify for Idaho's Retirement Benefits Deduction (Form 39R Line 8) once the recipient is 65+; statetax-2026-ID.json has no perSourceExemptions and pensionExemption is 'none', so the engine grants no deduction at all.

scenarios.name: single filer, military retired pay, age 63: Idaho's Retirement Benefits Deduction for service members uses a SEPARATE, more lenient age gate (62, or any age if disabled) than the general 65 threshold -- qualifies here where a CSRS pension at the same age would not
scenarios.source: Idaho Form 39R Instructions 2025 (EFO00088), page 7-8, 'Line 8e. The Idaho Retirement Benefits Deduction for Retired Service Members. You must meet at least one of the following: Classified as disabled (any age), or Age 62 or older, or...' -- a distinct, more lenient age test than Part One's general 65-or-62-disabled gate, which does not apply to Line 8e. RE-LABELLED IN TASK 8, and the re-label was value-neutral (measured: this case reports 1266.70 before and after, because Idaho ships no rule matching either label). This row read 'federalCivilian' only because the PlanSource enum had no case for military retired pay when this fixture was written. Phase 5b Task 1 ADDED that case, 'uniformedServices', and Task 8 moved this row onto it. Why it is load-bearing rather than tidy: Line 8e's service-member test (disabled at any age, or 62 or older) is MORE LENIENT than Part One's general 65-or-62-disabled gate, and every other CSRS row in this file (ID-1, ID-2, ID-4, ID-5) is on that general gate. While this row shared the 'federalCivilian' label with them, this case at 63 and ID-6 at 63 demanded CONTRADICTORY answers from one enum case, so no rule could satisfy both. They are now distinguishable. Task 8 nevertheless shipped NO Idaho rule, for reasons unrelated to the label: see Phase5bIdahoDecisionTests.swift. Arithmetic: standard deduction (age 63, under 65, no age addition, no OBBBA bonus) = $16,100 base only. $40,000 - $16,100 = $23,900 before the retirement deduction. The $40,000 military pension is eligible up to the lesser of itself or $48,216, exceeding the $23,900 remaining, flooring taxable income at $0. Tax = $0.00.

knownDefect.summary: Retired service members qualify for Idaho's Retirement Benefits Deduction at age 62 (not 65) per Form 39R Line 8e, a distinct gate from Part One's general rule; the engine has no age-tiered or per-source retirement deduction of any kind for ID, granting nothing. PHASE 5 WARNING: this file's only under-62 case is ID-1 (age 60), so a single age-62 gate applied to (federalCivilian, definedBenefit) would turn all five ID cases in this file green while encoding 62 as the CSRS civilian gate too, when the real CSRS gate is 65 (ID-2's own citation, Form 39R Part One). A green ID suite does NOT mean Idaho's age gates are correct.

scenarios.name: MFJ, both spouses 68/70 with CSRS pensions totaling $80,000, which is above the $72,324 MFJ maximum but the cap DOES NOT BIND observably here because taxable income floors at $0 either way -- see ID-8 for the case that does bind
scenarios.source: Idaho Form 39R Instructions 2025 (EFO00088), page 7, Line 8a: 'Married filing jointly...$72,324' maximum for 2025. Arithmetic: standard deduction (both 65+, MAGI $80,000 under $150,000 MFJ threshold) = $32,200 base + $1,650 x 2 age-65 additions + $6,000 x 2 full OBBBA senior bonuses = $47,500. $80,000 - $47,500 = $32,500 before the retirement deduction. Combined CSRS pensions of $80,000 are eligible only up to the $72,324 MFJ cap, which still exceeds the $32,500 remaining and floors taxable income at $0. Tax = $0.00.

knownDefect.summary: Both spouses' CSRS pensions qualify for the MFJ Retirement Benefits Deduction (capped at $72,324); the engine grants nothing, taxing the full $80,000 household income.

scenarios.name: MFJ, one spouse's CSRS pension qualifies (age 68) and the other spouse's private pension does not (age 55, and private pensions are never on Idaho's qualifying list regardless of age): one spouse qualifies
scenarios.source: Idaho Form 39R Instructions 2025 (EFO00088), page 7-8, Part Two 'Qualified Retirement Benefits' -- a closed list (CSRS/FSRDS, PERSI firefighters, certain Idaho police, retired service members); a private-employer pension is not on it at any age. Arithmetic: standard deduction (primary 68, 65+; spouse 55, not 65+; MAGI $70,000 under thresholds) = $32,200 base + $1,650 age-65 addition (primary only) + $6,000 OBBBA senior bonus (primary only) = $39,850. $70,000 - $39,850 = $30,150 before the retirement deduction. The $40,000 CSRS pension is eligible up to the lesser of itself or $72,324, exceeding the $30,150 remaining, flooring taxable income at $0; the $30,000 private pension is not eligible at all but the floor already reached $0 regardless. Tax = $0.00.

knownDefect.summary: Only the CSRS spouse's pension should be deductible; the engine grants no retirement deduction at all for ID, taxing the full $70,000 household income.

scenarios.name: single filer, CSRS pension, age 63 (between 62 and 65, not disabled): DENIED, because Part One's general gate is 65 and only the disabled reach it at 62 -- the discriminating case that separates a 62 gate from a 65 gate
scenarios.source: Idaho Form 39R Instructions 2025 (EFO00088), page 7, 'Line 8 Retirement Benefits Deduction', 'Part One - Age, Disability, and Marital/Filing Status': 'The recipients must be at least age 65 or be classified as disabled and be at least age 62.' At age 63 and NOT disabled, this taxpayer fails Part One, exactly as ID-1 does at 60. ADDED BY TASK 8 under shared-procedure Step 3 ('what would this rule wrongly match? If the fixture set has no case that would catch that, ADD one'). Phase 4 flagged that this file's only sub-65 CSRS case was ID-1 at age 60, so a single age-62 gate over (federalCivilian, definedBenefit) turned all five original cases green while encoding 62 as the CIVILIAN gate, when Part One's civilian gate is 65. That was MEASURED, not argued: a pooled pensionExemption with regularExemptionMinAge 62 was temporarily added to the shipped Idaho config and every one of ID-1 through ID-5 passed, while THIS case reported 0.00 against the 1266.70 Idaho law requires. The mutation was reverted. This case is what makes that rule unavailable to a future contributor. Its inputs are ID-3's inputs with one field changed, planSource federalCivilian instead of uniformedServices, which is the whole point: at the same age 63, Idaho denies the civilian and allows the service member, and the two are separable ONLY because Task 1 added the uniformedServices case. Arithmetic is ID-3's, unchanged: federal standard deduction (age 63, under 65, no age addition, no OBBBA senior bonus) = $16,100 base only. $40,000 - $16,100 = $23,900 taxable x 5.3% flat rate = $1,266.70.

scenarios.name: single filer, military retired pay, age 55 (below Line 8e's own 62 gate, not disabled): DENIED -- the guard that stops an UNGATED per-source military rule, the shape a rule-writer reaches for first
scenarios.source: Idaho Form 39R Instructions 2025 (EFO00088), page 7-8, 'Line 8e. The Idaho Retirement Benefits Deduction for Retired Service Members. You must meet at least one of the following: Classified as disabled (any age), or Age 62 or older, or...'. Line 8e is more lenient than Part One but it is NOT ageless: at 55 and not disabled this retiree fails 8e's own test and deducts nothing. ADDED BY TASK 8 under Step 3, guarding a DIFFERENT wrong rule from ID-6's. The model's per-source rules carry no age field at all (PerSourceExemptionRule has matchSources, matchStructures and treatment, nothing else) and TaxCalculationEngine.applyRetirementExemptions applies a matched rule 'UNCONDITIONALLY (no age gate)', so the obvious way to give ID-3 its lenient gate -- a perSourceExemptions rule matching uniformedServices with treatment full -- exempts military retired pay at EVERY age. That was MEASURED too: with that rule temporarily added to the shipped Idaho config, ID-3 passed and this case reported 0.00 against 1266.70. The mutation was reverted. This case matters because the population it protects is not marginal: a service member retiring at 20 years is routinely in their early forties, so the ungated rule is wrong for most military retirees for two decades each, in the under-taxation direction. Arithmetic: federal standard deduction (age 55, no age addition, no OBBBA senior bonus) = $16,100 base only. $40,000 - $16,100 = $23,900 taxable x 5.3% flat rate = $1,266.70.

scenarios.name: MFJ, both spouses 68/70 with CSRS pensions totaling $140,000: the cap BINDS observably, separating a correct $72,324 maximum from an uncapped deduction
scenarios.source: Idaho Form 39R Instructions 2025 (EFO00088), page 7, Line 8a: 'Married filing jointly...$72,324' maximum for 2025. ADDED BY TASK 8 REVIEW under shared-procedure Step 3. ID-4 is NAMED a cap straddle but cannot test one: at its $80,000 of pensions, taxable income before the deduction is only $32,500, so it floors at $0 whether the deduction is capped at $72,324 or left uncapped at $80,000, and both a correct rule and a cap-less rule produce ID-4's published $0.00. This case raises the pensions until the difference is visible on the tax line. Arithmetic: standard deduction (both 65+, MAGI $140,000 under the $150,000 MFJ threshold, so both OBBBA senior bonuses are full) = $32,200 base + $1,650 x 2 age-65 additions + $6,000 x 2 senior bonuses = $47,500. $140,000 - $47,500 = $92,500 before the retirement deduction. Combined CSRS pensions of $140,000 are eligible only up to the $72,324 MFJ maximum, so $92,500 - $72,324 = $20,176 taxable x 5.3% flat rate = $1,069.33. An UNCAPPED rule would subtract the full $140,000 and floor taxable income at $0.00, so this case is what separates the two. The engine grants no Idaho retirement deduction at all today, so it currently taxes the whole $92,500.

knownDefect.summary: Both spouses' CSRS pensions qualify for the MFJ Retirement Benefits Deduction, capped at $72,324; the engine grants nothing, taxing the full $92,500 of post-standard-deduction income. Same mechanism as ID-4, but this case additionally pins the CAP: a rule that granted the deduction UNCAPPED would report $0.00 here and would still pass ID-4, so this is the only Idaho case that can tell a correct $72,324 maximum from no maximum at all.
